verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, of David. In YHWH I have taken refuge. How will you say to my soul: Flee, [to] your mountain, [O] bird?
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster; a song of David. In the LORD I have taken refuge, and I stand there still. So how can you say to me, to my very soul, "Fly! Away to your mountain, little bird"?
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a psalm of a man under pressure, and the first line is a refusal. Your actors should hear the contrast between 'I have taken refuge' (a settled act, perfect tense) and the taunt that follows. The voice addressed is plural ('you say') while the soul he speaks of is his own. Who the speakers are is the first decision to make. Ibn Ezra takes them to be his enemies and the wicked, whom he addresses directly, and Radak makes them the informers who told Saul where he was hiding; Meiri ties the scene to the men of Keilah, who meant to hand him over. Only on a looser reading would they be friendly advisers urging him to run, and the verse itself does not say. Later readers set it in David's flight from Saul.

The KJV 'put I my trust' is softer than the Hebrew: חסה is physical, 'to shelter in the shadow of', the way a bird hides under a rock. 'A Psalm of David' is also the KJV's addition. The Hebrew has only 'of David', plus the title 'to the choirmaster', the only musical direction on the page. The line 'Flee as a bird to your mountain' is the KJV's smoothing: the Hebrew has no 'as', just 'your mountain, bird' (Ibn Ezra and Radak note the missing kaf). The insult is that he is told to be a bird, a thing that runs from every shadow. The Qere נודי is addressed to the soul as a woman; the Ketiv נודו is plural, and Rashi hears all of Israel told the same thing by the nations.

philological_notes.note: 'Flee, wander off': the verb is used of a bird that leaves its nest (Prov 27:8). The Ketiv is נוּדוּ (plural), the Qere נוּדִי (feminine singular, addressed to the 'soul', nefesh, which is a feminine noun). The word is a push away, not a plan.
'I have taken refuge': it describes the act of running for shelter, with the idea of protection under a covering. The perfect tense marks an act already done and still in force.
'To the choirmaster / overseer'. A direction to the one in charge of the music, from the root 'to excel, to oversee'. Of the versions here, only YLT's 'Overseer' keeps the idea of supervision.

token_glosses.gloss: flee, you (Qere; Ketiv נודו, 'you all flee')

verses.translation_literal: For behold, the wicked tread [the] bow, they have set their arrow upon [the] string, to shoot in [the] darkness at [the] upright of heart.
verses.translation_dramatic: Look! The wicked are bending the bow. The arrow is already set against the string, and they are aiming it into the dark, at those whose hearts are straight.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Behold' is the actors' cue to point. The speaker is giving the advisers' reasons, and they are urgent: the danger is happening now. The verbs set the tempo, a present 'tread' followed by a completed 'they have prepared', so the arrow is already on the string.

The KJV says 'bend their bow', which is accurate in effect, but the Hebrew דרך is 'tread': a strong composite bow was braced by standing on one end, and a fighter puts his foot on it to string it (Rashi). The listener is meant to see the foot on the wood. 'Privily' in the KJV is archaic for 'in the darkness' (במו אפל), and the Hebrew says darkness; the dark is both cover and the moral color of the shot. 'Upright of heart' means straight, not twisted, in the inner life. Jeremiah 9:2 uses the same image of the bow as the tongue, and Rashi reads it that way here too, since slander is also an arrow. Later readers name the archers as Doeg and the informers (Rashi, Metzudat David).

philological_notes.note: 'They tread': used of stepping on the bow to string it. The -ן ending is an archaic energic form of the imperfect. Rashi explains the verb as the foot on a hard bow.
'In darkness'. בְּמוֹ is a poetic form of 'in'. Rashi and Radak read it as 'in secret'; the Hebrew says darkness.
'String, cord': the bowstring, as in the 'seven fresh cords' of Judges 16:7 (Metzudat Zion cites the verse). Rashi gives the French 'corde'.

verses.translation_literal: For [if] the foundations are torn down, [the] righteous [one] — what has he done?
verses.translation_dramatic: If the foundations themselves are pulled down, what is left for the righteous to do? What has the righteous man ever achieved?
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the advisers' last argument, and it is a good one: when the structure falls, virtue is useless. The line is short and is spoken in despair. The Hebrew is clipped, with no verb between 'the righteous' and 'what', so the actor can leave a gap.

The KJV 'what can the righteous do?' makes it a question about ability. The Hebrew verb is a perfect, 'what has he done / what did he accomplish?', and the sense can be either 'what good did righteousness do?' or 'what has the righteous done to deserve this?' (Rashi, Meiri). The word for foundations, שתות, is rare and the KJV 'destroyed' is weaker than הרס, which is used of pulling down walls and altars. Ibn Ezra and Radak also give 'nets' for the noun, so the verse might speak of schemes being undone, but the building image is the most natural, and the one the later poem answers by taking us up to the heavenly temple in verse 4. 'Foundations' stands for law, order and the just men who hold society up. Ancient listeners knew a city's life depended on its foundation stones; the psalm's fear is that the moral base is gone.

philological_notes.note: 'The foundations': a rare plural. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat Zion link it to Isa 19:10, where the same word means a base, and the commentators also offer 'nets' as an alternative.
'They are torn down', niphal of הרס, which describes the demolition of walls and altars; the force is stronger than 'destroyed'.
A perfect: 'what has he done / accomplished?' Not 'what can he do', which would need a different form.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH [is] in [the] temple of his holiness; YHWH — in the heavens [is] his throne. His eyes see; his eyelids test [the] sons of Adam.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the LORD is in his holy temple. The LORD, whose throne is set in the heavens. His eyes are open and watching; even his eyelids, narrowed, weigh and test every son of Adam.
verses.directors_commentary:
The pace changes here: this is the answer, and the actors should slow and drop their voices. After the panic of verses 1 to 3 the poet gives two statements in parallel, the temple and the throne, and the name YHWH is spoken twice at the head of each clause. The advisers have said that the foundations are gone; the speaker replies that the one who counts is still enthroned. Whether 'his holy temple' is the Jerusalem temple or heaven itself is disputed (Radak takes the temple to be heaven), and the doubling here suggests both are meant: the sanctuary on earth and the throne above.

The KJV 'his eyes behold, his eyelids try' is correct, but the Hebrew picture is more physical. The eyelids are what one narrows to look closely, so 'eyelids test' means he squints at us as a goldsmith looks at metal. בחן is a metal-assayer's word. 'The children of men' is the Hebrew 'sons of Adam', all humanity, with no limit to Israel. The KJV also writes 'the Lord's throne is in heaven' with a possessive and so breaks the double YHWH; the Hebrew stands with the name twice, a deliberate stress against the idea that the LORD has gone away. As Rashi puts it, however high the throne, his eyes see you on earth.

philological_notes.note: 'His eyelids'. The word is reduplicated from the root 'to fly, flutter'. Its use in an image of divine testing is unusual: even the narrowing of the lid is part of God's scrutiny. Metzudat Zion glosses it as the pupil of the eye.
'They test, examine': the word is used of assaying metal. The verb is plural with a plural subject 'eyelids'. The verse sets 'see' beside 'test': seeing is passive, testing is not.
'The temple of his holiness'. Radak says the temple is heaven, Rashi sees the heights of the throne above with eyes on the earth below.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH tests [the] righteous, and [the] wicked and [the] lover of violence — his soul hates.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD tests the righteous. But the wicked, the man who loves violence? The LORD's own soul hates him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first half is a surprise to a modern ear and the actors must not rush it: the testing falls on the righteous. The wicked are not tested, and in Rashi's picture the flax-beater who strikes good flax hard but bad flax lightly makes the point. Divine testing is a sign of trust, not abandonment. The second half is blunt and the verb comes last: 'hates his soul', with the object stacked in front of it.

The KJV 'trieth' is archaic but accurate, and 'his soul hateth' keeps the Hebrew, which is startling in a text that avoids speaking of God's feelings: the nefesh here is the LORD's own throat and self, the seat of his appetite and his will, and the feminine verb agrees with it. Some versions (BBE) turn it into 'he has hate in his soul', a paraphrase that loses the verb coming last. The word חמס, 'violence', is more than physical harm; it means a wrong done to the weak, the outrage that in Genesis 6 brought the flood. The 'lover of violence' is someone who delights in it, in contrast to the 'lover of righteousness' who appears in verse 7: the psalm is built from two kinds of love.

philological_notes.note: 'He tests': God assays the righteous as a smith tests metal. Radak links it to Prov 3:12 (God reproves those he loves); Rashi gives the flax image from Genesis Rabbah.
'Violence, wrong': the injustice done by the strong to the weak. It is wider than the physical meaning of 'violence'.

'His soul hates': the verb is feminine, agreeing with נפש, so the subject is God's own self or desire. Rashi takes it as God's soul hating the wicked, and storing up the reward for their sins for the long age to come. Radak also makes God's soul the subject, but reads the hating as a refusal: God's soul hates (refuses) to reprove the wicked, who would not accept reproof, so he leaves them alone until their time comes and then destroys them.

verses.translation_literal: He will rain upon [the] wicked snares, fire and sulfur, and a wind of scorching heat — [the] portion of their cup.
verses.translation_dramatic: On the wicked he will make it rain: traps, fire, and sulfur, and a wind that scorches the breath from the air. That is what the cup holds for them. That is their portion.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb is the one that matters: 'he will rain', ימטר. The same root is used in Genesis 19:24, where the LORD 'rained' sulfur and fire on Sodom, so the listener's mind is already in a burning city. Play the first word as a sky darkening, then the list as one object after another falling. The final two words are small and low, a closing of the lid.

The KJV 'he shall rain snares, fire and brimstone' keeps the order, but 'brimstone' (a word that means 'burning stone') is only old English for sulfur, the Hebrew גפרית. 'An horrible tempest' replaces 'a wind of zil'afot': a zil'afah is not a storm. The word is rare and its sense is split: 'burning' (Rashi) or 'trembling', the shudder of Ps 119:53 (Ibn Ezra, Metzudat Zion), and Radak allows both. The literal layer says 'scorching heat', the dramatic layer follows Rashi, and a wind that makes one shake would also fit. The snares are odd after fire and sulfur, and commentators read them as nets, coals or hot plates (Rashi, Ibn Ezra) but the plain sense is a hunter's trap raining from the sky, the trappers trapped. The 'cup' is the share of drink handed to a guest at a feast (compare Ps 16:5, 'the portion of my cup'), here a cup of judgment: the wicked get their allotment, and it is measured.

philological_notes.note: 'He will rain': a causative, 'he will make it rain'. The same verb appears in Gen 19:24 (the rain of sulfur and fire on Sodom).
'Scorching heat'. Rashi reads 'burning'; Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion read 'trembling', both citing Ps 119:53; Radak gives both senses. Whether it is shuddering or heat is not settled.
'The portion of their cup': 'portion' and 'cup' both mean an allotted share. Radak compares Ps 16:5 and the pairing of two nouns of the same sense, as in 'dust of earth'.

verses.translation_literal: For righteous [is] YHWH; righteous deeds he loves. [The] upright — they behold his face.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the LORD is righteous, and he loves righteous things. The upright will see his face.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends on the other love: after 'the lover of violence' in verse 5 comes the one who loves justice, and it is God himself. 'For' (כי) closes the argument. The foundations are not lost, because the one who is righteous is on the throne. Play this one warm and quiet; after the burning of verse 6 the actors should lower their volume and breathe out.

The KJV 'his countenance doth behold the upright' reads 'his face' as the subject, which is the plain grammar of the Hebrew if we take the suffix as God's, but the verb יחזו is plural, and פנימו has an archaic ending (-מו) that Radak and Meiri read as 'his face', the way עלימו means 'upon him'. The commentators split. Meiri and Radak's first reading keep God's face as the subject: his face watches the upright, as the KJV has it. Metzudat David and Radak's alternative (citing Ps 17:15, 'I shall behold your face') make the upright the ones who see his face, as ASV and BBE do; seeing God's face is the supreme reward in the Psalms. Radak adds that the -מוֹ ending could be a true plural, 'their faces'. The plural צדקות, 'righteous acts', is a plural of fullness: every kind of righteousness. Nothing in the Hebrew says 'loveth' is only a feeling; as in the first verse of the psalm, God's love is a practical one that shelters.

philological_notes.note: 'Righteous deeds': a plural, so the psalm speaks of acts of justice, not an abstract virtue. Radak and Meiri read it as 'a man of righteous deeds' (like 'I am prayer', Ps 109:4).
'His/their faces': the archaic ending -מוֹ is read as a singular 'his face' by Radak and Meiri, who compare 'upon him' (עלימו). Radak also gives the plural, 'the faces of the righteous behold God'.
'Upright, straight': in this psalm it echoes 'upright of heart' in verse 2, the target of the arrows who now see God's face. Ibn Ezra takes it as a descriptive adjective ('the upright judgment').
